name: Squatmaxxing / spinal loading

card.summary: Squat-focused leg training; discussed for physique proportions, with no source tying it to height.
card.note: Wikipedia notes torso over-flexion raises lower-back forces; no height effect is documented.

quick.overview:
Squatmaxxing means training squats to build the legs and improve physique proportions. A looksmax.org thread discusses whether it suits wide-waisted people.

Sources describe the squat's muscles and injury considerations but do not link it to height.
quick.mechanism: The squat loads the legs and glutes while the spinal muscles and abdominals stabilise the trunk, which also compresses the spine under weight.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes that poor form, especially over-flexing the torso, raises lower-back forces and can risk disc herniation.

lead: Squatmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for building the legs and lower body through squats, to improve physique proportions: bigger quads and glutes, a stronger-looking lower half and a more balanced silhouette against the upper body.[1][2] It is discussed alongside gym-based physique work, in threads such as a looksmax.org thread titled Squatmaxxing that asks whether leg development suits people with a wide waist.[1]

The squat is a compound exercise whose primary movers are the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, adductor magnus and soleus, with the spinal erectors, abdominals and obliques acting as stabilizers.[2] Wikipedia describes it as building strength and size in the legs and hips and as a staple of powerlifting and recreational programs.[2]

The related phrase spinal loading refers to compression of the spine under weight. Wikipedia notes that measured height varies over the day and that exercise just before measuring can lower the reading,[3] and a 2023 review in European Spine Journal catalogues the mechanical loading of the spine in physical activities.[4] None of the sources describe squatting as changing adult stature.

Spinal loading is the other half of the topic. Heavy squats put load through the spine, and a small laboratory literature has measured the temporary loss of stature that follows loaded lifting, with changes of a few millimetres in a session; this is the same kind of daily height fluctuation that Wikipedia describes for ordinary activity.[3][9]

chain: Progressive squat training loads legs and glutes
Quads, glutes and hips add muscle
angle.text: Squats train the largest muscles of the lower body, so regular training adds leg and glute size and a stronger-looking base for the physique. Looksmaxxing users discuss it for proportion; effects on height are not described in the sources.

infobox: Back squat (high-bar, low-bar), front squat, hack, Zercher, Bulgarian split squat[2]
Measured stature change after a weight-training circuit
About 3 mm in a small stadiometer study[9]

paras: Wikipedia describes the squat as a lower-body exercise with many variants: barbell back squats (high-bar or low-bar), front squats, overhead and Zercher squats, hack and machine squats, unilateral forms such as the Bulgarian split squat, and bodyweight versions such as goblet and air squats.[2] The Zercher and Steinborn variants are named after early strength athletes.[2]

Technique guidance in the article covers bar placement, bracing, depth and alignment. It notes that a bar pad can reduce direct pressure on the spine, particularly for beginners with less muscle cushioning, and that power cages and safety bars reduce risk.[2]

Wikipedia traces several variants to named strength athletes: the hack squat, from the German Hacke meaning heel, was popularised in English-speaking countries by the wrestler George Hackenschmidt in his 1908 book The Way to Live; the Zercher squat, with the bar in the crooks of the elbows, is named after the 1930s strongman Ed Zercher; and the Steinborn squat, begun from the floor without a rack, is named after Henry Milo Steinborn.[2] The baithak, or Hindu squat, was a staple of Indian wrestlers, including the Great Gama, and Bruce Lee reportedly used it in his training.[2]

In competition, powerlifters often use a low bar position for leverage while weightlifters use a high bar closer to the clean and jerk; the International Powerlifting Federation's standard for depth requires the hip crease to drop below the top of the knee.[2] Wikipedia lists records such as Paul Anderson's 421.5 kg raw squat in 1965 and records in multiple classes of raw and equipped lifting.[2]

Muscles named as primary movers are the quadriceps femoris, gluteus maximus, adductor magnus and soleus; stabilisers include the erector spinae, rectus abdominis, obliques, hamstrings, gluteus medius and minimus and gastrocnemius.[2]

The article lists barbell variants (back, front, hack, overhead, Zercher, Steinborn), single-leg and split variants such as the pistol and the Bulgarian split squat, equipment-based forms (belt, goblet, Smith machine, trap bar, safety squat bar) and bodyweight versions (air, jump, sissy and sumo squats); chains and bands vary resistance across the range of motion, and partial repetitions are used to work past sticking points.[2] Depth research reported there includes Jaberzadeh and colleagues (2016), who found the 0 to 50 degree range best targets the quadriceps without aggravating the patellofemoral joint, and Richards (2008), who reported that single-limb squats on a 16-degree decline maximised knee-extensor activation with less ankle stress.[2]

For physique purposes, people talk about adding different variants to emphasise quadriceps, glutes or adductors, which are the muscles named as primary movers.[2] This is the sense in which squatmaxxing is linked to leg size and proportion.

Members of looksmax.org have asked whether squatmaxxing and building the legs is worthwhile for people with a wide waist. One user describes legs very large relative to the upper body, and another replies asking for body fat percentage, gym history and height before advising.[1] The discussion is about proportion and physique, similar to how other gym-focused entries treat training.

The word spinal loading in the entry title reflects forum debates about whether heavy axial loading affects height, a question the biomechanics literature addresses only through reviews of spinal loading and disc behaviour.[4][7]

Resistance-trained athletes use squat variations to build the quadriceps, glutes and adductors, which are the primary movers named in descriptions of the lift.[2] Wikipedia notes that raising the heels reduces the gluteal contribution, so setups differ in which muscles they emphasise.[2]

A 2024 trial by Enes and colleagues, discussed by Stronger By Science, randomised 24 recreationally trained women to 12 weeks of front or back squatting twice a week. Thigh muscle thickness increased similarly in both groups, while the back-squat group improved more on a 45-degree leg-press strength test, which the authors attributed to heavier loading and greater hip flexion.[10] The commentator suggested the back squat may emphasise the glutes and adductors more and the front squat the quadriceps and back extensors more.[10]

Wikipedia also cites Kraemer and Ratamess (2005) on acute hormonal responses to squatting, with testosterone rising in men and growth hormone in women, and Myer and colleagues (2014) on squats strengthening the lower body after joint injury.[2]

Wikipedia reports that height varies across the day and that exercise just before a measurement lowers the reading; a typical measurement error with a stadiometer is about half a centimetre.[3] The mechanism behind loaded-exercise shrinkage is a short-term decrease in the height of the intervertebral discs under compression.[9]

Bourne and Reilly (British Journal of Sports Medicine, 1991) measured stature with a stadiometer sensitive to 0.01 mm in eight men aged about 25 before and after a six-exercise circuit of three sets of ten repetitions, done with and without a weightlifting belt. Stature fell by 3.59 mm without the belt and 2.87 mm with it, a difference that was not statistically significant, while participants reported significantly less discomfort with the belt.[9] The study examined a circuit rather than squats alone.

Spine-biomechanics reviews describe how load passes through the vertebrae and discs, and a 2005 controlled study examined body mass as a factor in stature change.[4][5][6] No source located examines squatting as a cause of lasting change in adult height; the measured effects described are short-term and fluctuate with the time of day and recent activity.[3][9] Height-focused looksmaxxing users sometimes ask whether heavy axial loading shortens stature over time, and the published material addresses the short-term component.[1]

Wikipedia warns that over-flexing the torso greatly increases forces on the lower back and may risk disc herniation, while noting that padding and bracing are used to reduce spinal contact.[2] It cites a 2013 review by Hartmann and colleagues concluding that deep squats with proper technique did not increase degenerative knee injury rates and that shallower squats may be associated with long-term degeneration of the lumbar spine and knees; the article carries a maintenance tag on source reliability.[2] A review of intervertebral disc mechanobiology links disc degeneration to extreme spinal loading regimens.[7]

Wikipedia lists common form errors as descending too quickly, over-flexing the torso, letting the knees collapse inward and lifting the heels, and recommends safeguards such as bar pads, power cages, safety squat bars and wrist straps; it also notes that squats are used in physical therapy because they build stability without excessive tibiofemoral compression.[2] A 2026 review of age-related spinal kyphosis discusses spinal curvature in older adults in relation to osteoporosis and sarcopenia, a separate topic from stature change due to lifting.[8]

The article also reports that deeper squats reduce cruciate ligament forces at high flexion while compressive forces on the menisci and cartilage peak at the same angles, and that the relative safety of deep versus shallow squats is hard to judge.[2]

Wikipedia cites Hartmann and colleagues (2013) concluding that deep squats with proper technique did not increase degenerative knee injury rates, and Jaberzadeh and colleagues (2016) reporting higher patellofemoral compressive loads in deeper squats.[2]
No studies found on squatting as a means of affecting height or appearance proportions in the sense used by looksmaxxing communities.

Related research includes a 1991 stadiometer study of temporary stature loss after a weight-training circuit, a 2024 randomised trial of front versus back squat training in women with similar thigh-muscle growth in both groups, and reviews of spinal loading and disc mechanobiology.[9][10][4][7]

timeline.event: George Hackenschmidt's book The Way to Live popularises the hack squat in English-speaking countries.[2]
Ed Zercher gives his name to the Zercher squat.[2]
Paul Anderson records a 421.5 kg squat.[2]
Hartmann and colleagues' review on deep squats and knee degeneration.[2]
Bourne and Reilly report about 3 mm of temporary stature loss after a weight-training circuit, with and without a belt.[9]
A randomised trial of front versus back squat training in women reports similar thigh-muscle growth in both groups.[10]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, squatmaxxing appears in a thread on whether leg training is useful for people described as wide-waisted.[1]

claims.claim: Squatting and leg development help people who are wide-waisted.
claims.believers: The thread poster asks if squatmaxxing and developing the legs is legitimate for this group; one user describes very large legs relative to the upper body, and another asks for body fat percentage and height before advising.[1]
claims.experts: No published studies were located on squatting for waist-to-leg proportion as an appearance goal; Wikipedia covers the exercise's muscles and injury considerations.[2]

claims.claim: Heavy squatting compresses the spine and can reduce height.
claims.believers: Height-focused users ask whether heavy axial loading shortens stature over time.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that exercise just before measuring lowers the reading; no source reviewed states that squatting changes adult stature.[3][2]

claims.claim: Heavy squats and axial loading compress the spine and can shorten you permanently.
claims.believers: Height-focused users on looksmaxxing forums ask whether loading the spine under heavy bars costs stature.[1]
claims.experts: Laboratory work measures a few millimetres of temporary shrinkage after a loaded circuit, comparable in kind to daily height variation; no located study measures lasting change in adult stature from squatting.[9][3]

claims.claim: A weightlifting belt reduces spinal shrinkage.
claims.believers: Lifters commonly use belts to stabilise the trunk during heavy squats.[9]
claims.experts: In the 1991 small study, stature loss was 3.59 mm without a belt and 2.87 mm with one, a difference that was not statistically significant, and discomfort was significantly lower with the belt.[9]

claims.claim: Front squats build quads while back squats build glutes.
claims.believers: Lifters choose variants to target the quadriceps or the glutes.[2]
claims.experts: A 12-week trial in women found similar thigh-muscle growth with front and back squats, and a commentator suggests different emphasis on glutes and quadriceps between them.[10]
